opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, because perception is one of those things that sounds like an obvious win. Of course the robot should see where it's going. But in practice it brings a lot of cost, and you have to be honest about whether the benefit is worth it for what you're trying to do.

On the benefit side, it's pretty clear. A blind policy can be surprisingly robust. You can train a quadruped that walks over rough terrain, recovers from slips, even climbs some steps purely from proprioception, the joint encoders and the IMU. But it's fundamentally reactive. It only learns about the step when it hits it with its foot. So it has to be conservative: lift the feet high, walk slowly, basically probe the world. With perception, even something as simple as a height map sampled around the robot, the policy can anticipate. It can place its feet deliberately, take stairs at a normal speed, jump onto a box, cross gaps. Things that are basically impossible blind.

The cost is mostly on the sim-to-real side. Proprioception transfers relatively well because joint positions in simulation look a lot like joint positions on the real robot. Perception doesn't. In simulation your height map is perfect. On the real robot it comes from depth cameras or lidar fused into an elevation map, and it's noisy, it has holes, it lags, it drifts when the state estimation drifts, and things like grass, snow, or reflective surfaces look completely wrong. A policy that fully trusts its perception will happily step into a hole that isn't there, or onto a step that's actually tall grass.

So a lot of the work is making the policy robust to bad perception. In training we add heavy noise and corruption to the height samples: offsets, missing patches, drift, sometimes outright wrong terrain. That forces the policy to learn when to trust its eyes and when to fall back on what it feels through its legs. Ideally you get the best of both: when perception is good, it moves efficiently and anticipates; when it's bad, it degrades gracefully toward the blind behavior instead of failing catastrophically.

Then there's the engineering cost. Training is slower because you have to simulate the sensors, or at least the height scans, for thousands of parallel robots. The observation space gets bigger, so the networks get bigger. And on the robot you now depend on a whole mapping pipeline that can fail on its own.

So my rule of thumb is: start blind, push it as far as it goes, and add perception when the task really needs anticipation, like stairs at speed, parkour-style motions, or gaps. And when you add it, spend as much effort on modeling how the perception fails as on the perception itself. That's usually what decides whether it works in the real world.

r001.rationale: It says perception transfers poorly from simulation to reality, while proprioception transfers relatively well, and describes noisy real-world sensing as a sim-to-real cost.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a blind policy that reacts when its foot hits an obstacle with perception that lets the robot anticipate and place its feet deliberately.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one we went back and forth on a lot. The way I think about it is that perception buys you capability, but it costs you in a few different currencies at once, and you have to be honest about whether you actually need what you're buying.

So, start with the blind case. A proprioceptive policy, just joint positions, velocities, IMU, maybe the previous actions, is remarkably robust. We showed with the ANYmal work that you can get a robot walking over stairs, rubble, slippery surfaces, all without ever seeing the terrain, because the policy learns to react within a step or two of contact. The sim-to-real gap there is small. Joint encoders and IMUs are basically the same in simulation as in reality, so what you train is what you get. And training is cheap, you can run thousands of robots in parallel on one GPU and have a policy in minutes.

The moment you add a camera or a depth sensor, several things change. First, the sim-to-real gap gets a lot wider. Rendering is expensive, so you lose a big chunk of your simulation throughput, and even then the images don't look like the real world. Depth sensors have noise, missing returns on reflective or dark surfaces, motion blur, latency. None of that comes for free in sim, you have to model it, and you never model it perfectly. Second, your policy is now reasoning about things it can't directly verify. A blind robot can only be wrong about what it's touching. A seeing robot can be wrong about something three meters away, and it can commit to a plan based on that.

So the tradeoff is really: what are the situations where reacting isn't enough? Stepping gaps, large steps you need to prepare for, placing feet precisely on stepping stones, avoiding obstacles, anything where by the time your foot touches it, it's too late. For those, you need perception, there's no way around it. And when we did add it, the approach that worked for us was to keep the perception representation as simple and as sim-friendly as possible. A height map or an elevation scan around the robot, rather than raw images, so the gap between simulation and reality is in a space you can reason about and inject noise into in a principled way. And you keep the proprioceptive backbone, so that when the perception is wrong, the robot still has that reactive layer to fall back on.

The thing I'd caution against is adding perception because it feels like it should help. If the blind policy is already succeeding on your terrain, the perceptive one will probably be worse in the real world, because you've added a failure mode without removing one. You want to add it when you can point to a concrete class of failures and say, this is impossible without seeing ahead.

r001.rationale: The response says adding a camera or depth sensor makes the sim-to-real gap “a lot wider.”

r002.rationale: It explains perception lets the robot prepare for gaps, large steps, precise footholds, and obstacles before contact, when reacting would be too late.

astra-6.text:
I think the main tradeoff is that perception lets you anticipate what’s coming, but it also makes the problem much more complicated. With proprioception alone—joint positions, velocities, and the motion of the body—you can get a very robust locomotion policy. But the robot only reacts to terrain once it makes contact. If you want to choose where to step or prepare for an obstacle, you need information about the environment.

In simulation, it’s relatively easy to give the policy a clean description of the terrain. The difficult part is making that information representative of what the real robot will get. Sensors have noise, delays, and occlusions. So you can train a policy that performs very well in simulation but depends too much on information that isn’t reliable in reality.

The goal is to use perception when it helps, while retaining that robust behavior when the perception is wrong or unavailable. Whether the added complexity is worthwhile really depends on the terrain and the task.

r001.rationale: It explains that clean simulated perception can differ from real sensors because of noise, delays, and occlusions, causing a policy to rely on information unavailable or unreliable in reality. This communicates an enlarged sim-to-real gap.

r002.rationale: It says proprioception-only policies react after contact, while perception provides information to choose where to step or prepare for an obstacle.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the tradeoff is that perception gives you the ability to anticipate, but it also adds complexity and another source of error. With a policy that only uses proprioception, the robot has to react once it makes contact with something. That can work surprisingly well, and you avoid having to simulate a sensor and transfer that perception system to the real world.

But if you need to choose where to put your feet, or prepare for a large obstacle, then reacting after contact may be too late. Perception becomes much more valuable there. The challenge is making sure the policy can handle noisy, delayed, or missing observations, rather than depending on perfect terrain information from the simulator. So I would assess it in terms of the task: how much does looking ahead improve what the robot can do, and does that improvement survive the imperfections of the real sensor?

r001.rationale: It mentions the challenge of transferring perception to the real world and sensor imperfections, but does not state that adding perception enlarges the sim-to-real gap.

r002.rationale: It says perception lets the robot anticipate and choose foot placements or prepare for large obstacles, instead of reacting only after contact.
